academy.001: A good racing line is the foundation of pace. Build it before chasing speed.
academy.002: What is an apex, and why does it matter?
academy.003: Choosing a better apex can save 0.3–0.5s without changing your speed.
academy.004:
The apex is the point where your car comes closest to the inside of a corner.

**Geometric apex:** the midpoint of the corner; a useful starting point for a simple 90-degree turn.

**Late apex:** further towards the exit, allowing you to straighten the car earlier for acceleration.

An early apex can send the car wide on exit. The best choice depends on the corner and what follows it.
academy.005: Later apex → earlier acceleration → more speed on the straight
academy.006: An early apex can give a fast entry but a poor exit
academy.007: Many corners benefit from a later apex
academy.008: A starting point: place the apex around two-thirds through the corner
academy.010: A later apex (green) lets you apply the throttle earlier
academy.011: Drivers often turn towards the apex as soon as they finish braking. The entry looks good, but the exit suffers.
academy.012: Look through to the exit. Turn in later so the car is straighter when you accelerate.
academy.013: Drive 10 laps with an early apex and 10 with a later apex. Compare your speed at the end of the straight.
academy.014: In the telemetry, check where you reach full throttle relative to the apex.
academy.015: Why can a later apex be faster?
academy.017: You can accelerate earlier and carry more exit speed
academy.018: You turn the steering wheel less
academy.020: A later apex lets you straighten the car and accelerate earlier. Even with a slightly slower entry, acceleration can begin 0.2–0.4s sooner.
academy.022: A more measured approach to a corner sequence can save around 0.6s by improving the final exit.
academy.023:
Corners separated by only a short straight need to be planned together.

**Rule:** if a long straight follows the second corner, sacrifice the first to improve the second exit.

Treat an S-bend as one flowing manoeuvre rather than two unrelated turns.
academy.024: In a sequence, prioritise the exit that leads onto the longest straight
academy.025: Trade some entry speed for a stronger exit
academy.026: Treat an S-bend as one flowing manoeuvre
academy.029: Sacrifice the first corner to improve the exit onto the straight
academy.030: Trying to optimise every corner in a sequence independently.
academy.031: Plan backwards from the exit. Find the best apex for the final corner, then work back through the sequence.
academy.032: Drive five laps focusing on entry to the first corner, then five focusing on exit from the second. Compare the time through the whole sequence.
academy.033: In the telemetry, check whether you reach full throttle within the first 50m after the second corner.
academy.034: What matters most when two corners lead onto a long straight?
academy.035: A strong entry into the first corner
academy.036: A strong exit from the second corner
academy.039: A strong exit from the second corner improves acceleration along the straight that follows.
academy.040: Racing lines for different corner types
academy.041: There is no universal racing line. Different corner types call for different approaches.
academy.042:
**90-degree corner:** a conventional later apex is a useful starting point.

**Hairpin:** a wide entry and late rotation can improve the exit.

**Fast corner:** an apex closer to the geometric midpoint can help preserve momentum.

**Opening-radius corner:** an earlier apex may work as the track opens on exit. Adapt the line to the actual layout.
academy.043: Hairpins often favour a late apex
academy.044: Fast corners often favour an apex nearer the geometric midpoint
academy.045: An opening-radius corner can allow an earlier apex and throttle pickup
academy.046: Track gradients affect the best apex position
academy.048: Different corner types call for different apex positions
academy.049: Applying the same approach to every corner.
academy.050: Classify each corner before practising: hairpin, fast corner or opening-radius turn. Adapt your line accordingly.
academy.051: Choose three different corner types and deliberately try different apex positions.
academy.052: Upload a lap to APEX. Review three different corners: does your minimum speed suit each corner type?
academy.053: Where is a late apex in a hairpin?
academy.054: In the middle of the corner
academy.055: At the start of the corner
academy.058: A late apex can improve the exit from a hairpin, especially when a long straight follows. Use a wide entry and delay the main rotation.
academy.059: Practice: 20 laps focused on your racing line
academy.060: Understanding the line is only the start. Repetition builds the ability to drive it consistently.
academy.061:
Laps 1–5: warm up at around 85% pace and focus on your line.

Laps 6–10: explore a later apex without rushing the throttle.

Laps 11–15: concentrate on three key corners.

Laps 16–20: try to put the whole lap together.
academy.062: Build a repeatable line before adding speed
academy.063: Keep the first 10 laps at around 85% pace
academy.064: Change one thing at a time
academy.065: Upload your telemetry after the session
academy.066: Driving flat out immediately and ignoring your line.
academy.067: Drive the first 10 laps at around 85% pace. Concentrate entirely on your line.

academy.071: Braking is one of the most demanding driving skills and a major source of lost time.
academy.073: Braking 15–30m earlier than necessary can cost 0.3–0.5s in a heavy braking zone.
academy.074:
Your braking point is where you first press the brake pedal.

**Too early:** you lose time before the corner.

**Too late:** you cannot reduce speed enough and miss the apex.

**On target:** you preserve speed before braking and arrive at the apex at a manageable speed.
academy.075: Moving a braking point 10m later can save around 0.15s
academy.076: Choose a clear marker: a board, barrier detail or patch of asphalt
academy.077: Move your braking point forward gradually, by 2–3m
academy.078: Telemetry shows exactly where braking starts
academy.079: Braking 15m later increases speed on the approach
academy.080: Keeping a conservative braking point without ever testing it.
academy.081: Move the braking point forward in small steps. If you miss the apex, move it back and rebuild consistency.
academy.082: Spend 10 laps establishing a repeatable marker. Then test a point 5m later. If you overshoot, move it back by 2m.
academy.083: Find the first brake input in your telemetry and note your speed there. Compare it with the reference.
academy.084: How do you find a suitable braking point?
academy.085: Always brake at exactly the same place
academy.086: Move it forward gradually, then back slightly if you overshoot
academy.088: Always brake as late as possible
academy.089: Approach the limit in small steps. Once braking is too late to reach the apex reliably, move the marker back and confirm it over several laps.
academy.090: Brake pressure: how to use the pedal
academy.091: How you apply the brake matters as much as where. An inconsistent pressure profile can cost 0.1–0.2s.
academy.092:
**Stepped application:** pressure builds slowly, then jumps to the peak.

**Abrupt release:** strong initial braking ends with a sudden lift off the pedal, unsettling the car.

**A controlled profile:** build pressure decisively, hold it while needed, then reduce it progressively as you turn in. Match the peak pressure to the car, grip and speed.
academy.093: Build brake pressure decisively, then release it progressively
academy.094: Avoid hesitating during the initial brake application
academy.095: Progressive brake release begins the trail-braking phase
academy.096: In telemetry, examine the shape of the brake trace
academy.098: A clear rise followed by a progressive release
academy.099: Building pressure in steps instead of making one controlled application.
academy.100: Build initial pressure decisively, then release it smoothly towards the apex.
academy.101: Focus on one corner for five laps. Watch how consistently you reach peak brake pressure.
academy.102: The brake trace should show a clear rise followed by a smooth release.
academy.103: What should a controlled braking trace look like?
academy.104: A gradual rise followed by a sudden drop
academy.105: A clear rise followed by a smooth drop
academy.108: Initial braking transfers load towards the front. Progressive release helps you balance braking and steering during turn-in.
academy.109: Trail braking: braking into the corner
academy.110: Trail braking means continuing to brake as you begin turning, while progressively reducing pressure.
academy.111:
**Why it works:** braking transfers load towards the front tyres and can help the car rotate.

As steering input increases, reduce brake pressure to share the available grip between turning and slowing down.

**The limit:** asking for too much braking and cornering at once can cause the tyres to slide.
academy.112: Reduce brake pressure as you add steering
academy.113: Front load can help the car rotate
academy.114: Stay within the tyres’ combined grip limit
academy.115: Begin with a small amount of trail braking and build gradually
academy.117: Trail braking can improve corner entry
academy.118: Fully releasing the brake before beginning to turn.
academy.119: Begin reducing brake pressure just before turn-in, then continue releasing towards the apex.
academy.120: Choose one slow corner. Practise carrying a small amount of brake into the first part of the turn.
academy.121: In telemetry, the tail of the brake trace should overlap the start of the steering input.
academy.123: Braking with the rear of the car
academy.124: Continuing to brake while turning in
academy.127: Trail braking is a progressively reducing brake input during turn-in. It helps manage load transfer and rotation.
academy.129: Good throttle control builds exit speed and keeps the car balanced.
academy.131: Throttle application affects your speed for the next 200m of straight.
academy.132:
**Slow corner:** pick up the throttle around the apex, then build towards full power as the car straightens.

**Fast corner:** a small lift may be enough; avoid unnecessary interruption to acceleration.

**Hairpin:** wait until the car is ready to accept more power.

**Linked corners:** use partial throttle when needed to preserve the position for the next turn.
academy.133: Slower corners usually require more patience before full throttle
academy.134: Too much throttle too early can cause oversteer and cost speed
academy.136: The shape of the input matters as much as its starting point
academy.138: Match throttle application to the corner
academy.139: Using the same throttle profile in every corner.
academy.140: Identify the corner type and adapt your throttle application to its exit.
academy.141: Try three different throttle profiles in three different corner types. Record the session.
academy.142: Compare your exit speed 100m after the apex with the reference.
academy.143: Why can too much throttle too early be a problem in a slow corner?
academy.145: It can cause wheelspin and reduce grip
academy.148: The tyres are already using grip to turn. Adding too much power before unwinding the steering can cause wheelspin.
academy.150: Abrupt throttle application can cost around 0.1s in a slow corner through wheelspin.
academy.151:
**Abrupt throttle:** a sudden demand for acceleration can exceed the rear tyres’ available grip and cause wheelspin or oversteer.

**Progressive throttle:** begin with a smaller input and increase it as you unwind the steering.

In telemetry, look for a smooth ramp rather than a vertical jump. Adjust the rate to the car and available grip.
academy.152: Progressive throttle can improve exit time by 0.08–0.15s
academy.153: This is especially important in rear-wheel-drive cars
academy.154: As your feel improves, you can apply the throttle more quickly
academy.155: Look for a smooth throttle trace
academy.157: Smooth application helps maximise acceleration without wheelspin
academy.158: Stamping on the throttle at the apex can overwhelm the rear tyres.
academy.159: Start with a partial input at the apex and build smoothly towards full throttle as the car straightens.
academy.160: Focus on one slow corner for five laps. Count “one, two” as you build throttle pressure.
academy.161: Look for a smooth rise from zero to full throttle without repeated steps.
academy.163: Trail braking rewards precision. Too much brake while turning can quickly unsettle the car.
academy.164: Car balance: how braking loads the front
academy.165: Managing the car’s balance through the pedals is a key step towards advanced driving.
academy.166:
A car is a dynamic system: braking transfers load forwards, while acceleration transfers it rearwards.

**Under braking:** the front tyres carry more load, which can help the car rotate.

**As the brake is released:** that load reduces.

Trail braking controls this transition by maintaining a small, decreasing brake input as you turn in.
academy.167: Braking transfers load towards the front
academy.168: Acceleration transfers load towards the rear
academy.169: Trail braking manages front load during turn-in
academy.170: Releasing the brake changes the car’s balance
academy.172: Use the brake to manage front load and rotation
academy.173: Releasing the brake abruptly as you turn in.
academy.174: Reduce brake pressure progressively as you increase steering angle.
academy.175: Focus on the feeling of front load in one corner. Experiment with a small residual brake input through the first part of turn-in.
academy.176: In telemetry, look for a short overlap between brake release and the start of steering input.
academy.177: Why can trail braking help the car rotate?
academy.179: It maintains load on the front tyres
academy.182: Braking transfers load towards the front tyres. Managing that load through a progressive release can help the car rotate into the corner.
academy.184: A measured entry can produce a faster exit. Entering too quickly often delays acceleration.
academy.185:
**The sequence:** measured entry → later apex → earlier acceleration → faster exit.

**The trade-off:** losing 0.1s on entry may be worthwhile if it gains 0.4s on the following straight.

This matters most before a long straight, where exit speed affects the next 500–800m.
academy.186: A slower entry can pay off before a long straight
academy.187: Aim to gain more on exit than you give up on entry
academy.188: Prioritise the final corner before a long straight
academy.189: Do not apply the same rule blindly in the middle of a chicane
academy.191: A controlled entry enables earlier acceleration
academy.192: Carrying too much entry speed into a corner before a long straight.
academy.193: Deliberately reduce entry speed. Aim for a more accurate apex, earlier throttle and higher speed on the straight.
academy.194: At Monza’s final corner, try entering 5 km/h slower. Compare your speed 200m after the exit.
academy.195: Compare your speed at the start of the straight with the reference.
academy.196: Why can a slower entry produce a faster lap?
academy.198: It can allow earlier acceleration onto the straight
academy.200: It is easier for spectators to follow
academy.201: Exit speed carries down the following straight. The longer the straight, the more a good exit can matter.
academy.203: Telemetry turns impressions into evidence. Learn to read your data systematically.
academy.204: Lap time delta: reading time loss
academy.205: One trace shows where you lose time, how much and in which section.
academy.206:
The **delta trace** shows the time difference between your lap and the reference along the track.

- **Falling trace:** you are gaining time.
- **Rising trace:** you are losing time.
- **Flat trace:** the time gap is steady.

Look for the steepest rises to identify the sections to review next.
academy.207: Delta rises where you lose time and falls where you gain it
academy.208: The slope shows how quickly the gap changes
academy.209: Look for steep rises to find improvement opportunities
academy.210: Link each change in delta to a corner or straight
academy.212: Green indicates time gained; red indicates time lost
academy.213: Looking only at the final lap time without finding where time was lost.
academy.214: After each session, find the largest rise in the delta trace. Use it to choose your next practice focus.
academy.215: Upload your latest lap and identify the three sections with the largest increases in delta.
academy.216: Choose the corner with the largest loss and focus on it for the next 10 laps.
academy.217: What does a rapidly rising red delta mean?
academy.219: You are losing time quickly in this section
academy.220: There is a problem with the track
academy.222: A rising delta means you are losing time relative to the reference. A steeper rise means the loss is accumulating faster.
academy.223: Reading speed, throttle and brake traces
academy.224: Speed shows the result. Throttle and brake traces help explain how you got there.
academy.225:
**Three key channels:**

1. **Speed:** the result, such as low minimum speed at the apex.
2. **Brake:** where braking begins, how much pressure is used and how it is released.
3. **Throttle:** when power is applied and how progressively it builds.

Find a speed deficit, inspect the inputs in that section, then choose one technique change to test.
academy.226: Speed shows the result; throttle and brake inputs help explain it
academy.227: Look for causes rather than symptoms
academy.228: A reference lap reveals specific differences
academy.229: Change one thing at a time
academy.231: Read speed, throttle and brake together
academy.232: Looking only at speed while ignoring the inputs that produced it.
academy.233: Find a slow section, open the brake and throttle traces, then compare them with the reference.

academy.235: Upload two laps. In your slowest corner, how does your braking point differ from the reference?

academy.241: Low speed is a symptom. Checking the brake and throttle traces helps identify which inputs may have caused it.

**Step 2 — three minutes:** inspect the speed trace in that section. How large is the deficit?

academy.254: Focus and pressure management are part of race performance. Learn to practise them alongside driving technique.
academy.256: In a flow state, driving feels fluid and automatic. A consistent preparation routine can help you find that focus.
academy.257:
**Flow** is a state of deep focus where the challenge matches your skill.

Too easy: attention may drift. Too difficult: pressure can disrupt performance.

To prepare, warm up at a manageable pace, choose one focus and use steady breathing. Look for a rhythm where your actions feel deliberate but natural.
academy.258: Match the challenge to your current skill
academy.259: Warm up — the first five laps are not a time trial
academy.261: Before the session, try a four-second inhale and six-second exhale
academy.263: A manageable challenge helps you focus
academy.264: Trying to drive at the limit from the first lap.
academy.265: Warm up for five laps at around 85% pace with one clear focus, then build speed.
academy.266: Before the next session, spend three minutes settling your breathing, then drive three warm-up laps focused on your line.

academy.270: A mismatch between the challenge and your skill
academy.273: Flow is easier when the challenge matches your ability. Both boredom and excessive pressure can disrupt focus.
academy.274: Pressure and mistakes: protecting a good lap
academy.275: Your response to a mistake can matter as much as the mistake itself.
academy.276:
**The cycle:** mistake → frustration → lost focus → another mistake.

**Break it:**
1. Treat the mistake as information.
2. Take a breath before reacting.
3. Return to your chosen focus.
4. Do not try to recover the lost time immediately.

Start each lap with a fresh plan.
academy.277: A mistake is information, not failure
academy.278: Do not chase the time lost in a mistake
academy.280: A steady breath can help release tension
academy.281: Trying to compensate for a mistake by attacking the next lap harder.
academy.282: After a mistake, drive a controlled lap. Then analyse what happened and choose a correction.
academy.283: In a practice session, notice how you respond after a small mistake. Focus on returning to your normal rhythm.
academy.284: Find the lap after a clear mistake. Was it faster or slower than your average?
academy.285: A suitable setup can improve both pace and confidence. Learn to diagnose handling issues and test small changes.
academy.287: Wing angle trades straight-line speed against grip in fast corners.
academy.288:
**Rear wing:**
- More angle adds rear downforce and drag.
- Less angle reduces drag but may reduce rear stability.

**Monza:** long straights favour a lower-drag compromise.

**Tight circuits:** more downforce may be useful where straight-line speed matters less.

Keep the aerodynamic balance in mind: too little rear support can increase oversteer, while too much relative to the front can increase understeer.
academy.289: More wing generally means more downforce and drag
academy.291: Compare a lower-drag setup at Monza with your baseline at Spa
academy.292: Change one or two clicks at a time
academy.294: Wing angle trades downforce against straight-line speed
academy.295: Copying a setup without understanding it, or changing five to 10 clicks at once.
academy.296: Change one or two clicks. Record handling impressions and telemetry before and after.
academy.297: Compare runs with the baseline wing and two clicks less. Review speed on the straights and in fast corners.
academy.298: Compare your Monza and Spa setups, noting how rear-wing changes affect pace and stability.
academy.299: Why might you reduce wing angle at Monza?
academy.301: To reduce drag on the long straights

**Brake bias** determines the share of braking effort sent to each axle.

**Too far forward:** the front tyres may reach their limit first.

**Too far rearward:** rear lock-up can make the car unstable.

Start from the car’s baseline and use telemetry and handling feedback to test small adjustments. Suitable values vary between cars and conditions.

**Mental rehearsal** helps you practise attention, sequence and reference points away from the simulator.

1. Settle your breathing.
2. Imagine a lap in real time.
3. For each corner, rehearse the braking point, turn-in, apex and throttle pickup.
4. If you lose your place, restart from that corner.

Include the details you know: the view, sound, steering and pedal inputs.

1. Choose one specific skill.
2. Focus on it for 10 laps.
3. Review the telemetry.
4. Make one adjustment.
5. Drive another 10 laps.

A focused target and specific feedback make progress measurable.

academy.354: Tyre operating temperature: why it matters
academy.355: Cold or overheated tyres can cost substantial lap time and make the car harder to control.
academy.356:
Tyres perform best within an operating window that depends on the car, compound and simulator.

**Too cold:** grip is limited, so build load progressively.

**Too hot:** grip can fall and wear can accelerate.

**In the working window:** the tyres provide more consistent grip. Check the tyre model and guidance for your car rather than assuming one universal temperature target.
academy.357: Use the warm-up lap to build tyre temperature progressively
academy.358: Avoid abrupt inputs on the first lap
academy.359: Both underworking and sliding the tyres can compromise performance
academy.360: Compare corner speed as the tyres warm up
academy.362: Grip is most consistent within the tyre’s intended operating window

academy.373: Tyre degradation: pace over a full stint
academy.374: Five fast laps followed by 15 slow ones can be a poor trade-off.
academy.375:
**Degradation** is the loss of tyre performance through wear and thermal effects.

Overheating can produce a sharp drop in grip. Whether it recovers depends on the tyre model and the damage already done.

Smooth, repeatable inputs help avoid unnecessary sliding and heating. Aim to keep the tyres in a useful operating window for as much of the stint as possible.
academy.376: Abrupt inputs and sliding can overheat tyres
academy.377: A lock-up or slide can create a local temperature spike
academy.378: A steady pace is often better than repeated bursts and recovery laps
academy.379: Smooth driving helps manage heat and wear
academy.381: Smooth inputs help maintain consistent lap times

academy.383: Start slightly below your absolute limit, establish a steady rhythm, then push later if the tyres still have grip.

academy.387: Two drivers can get very different tyre life from the same car. Technique is one important reason.
academy.388:
**Inputs to review:**

1. **Wheelspin:** sliding under power generates heat.
2. **Heavy braking and lock-up:** concentrated braking stress can affect the fronts.
3. **Excess steering lock:** persistent understeer scrubs the front tyres.
4. **Abrupt steering:** sudden load changes can increase sliding.

Use telemetry to find repeated patterns rather than assuming every temperature change has the same cause.

academy.401:
**The first corner:** cars are close together, lines are restricted and grip may be lower than expected.

Leave space, anticipate earlier braking and avoid gaps that are closing.

Giving up one place while keeping the car intact can be better than risking the whole race for an opening-lap gain.

academy.418: Undercut and overcut: timing the pit stop
academy.419: A well-timed pit stop can gain positions without an on-track overtake.
academy.420:
**Undercut:** pit before a rival, then use the pace of fresh tyres to gain time before they stop.

**Overcut:** stay out longer and use clear track or stronger pace on your existing tyres while the rival completes their stop and out-lap.

The choice depends on tyre warm-up, degradation, traffic, pit loss and the gap between cars.

academy.422: An overcut uses pace gained by staying out longer

academy.430: Following a rival can reduce drag on a straight, but disturbed airflow may reduce grip in corners.
academy.431:
**Dirty air:** disturbed airflow behind another car can reduce aerodynamic performance, making fast corners harder.

**Slipstream:** following on a straight can reduce drag and improve speed.

Balance the straight-line benefit against cornering grip and visibility. The useful following distance depends on the car and circuit.

academy.433: Choose an attacking distance that preserves control and visibility

academy.443: Qualifying calls for a different balance of preparation and risk from a race stint.
academy.444:
**Race pace:** prioritise consistency and tyre life.

**Qualifying:** prepare the car and tyres for a focused flying lap.

Manage the out-lap, leave a useful gap and attack with a clear plan. If a mistake makes the lap unrepresentative, decide whether another attempt is worthwhile based on time remaining, traffic and tyre condition.

The peak-grip window depends on the tyre, car and conditions.

**Practice protocol:**
1. Build temperature on the out-lap without unnecessary sliding.
2. Use the next lap to establish grip and rhythm.
3. Attempt a flying lap when the tyres are ready.
4. Review the result and tyre condition before another attempt.

academy.474:
**Qualifying simulation:**
1. Set a 15-minute timer.
2. Leave the pits and prepare the tyres.
3. Make two flying-lap attempts.
4. Regroup after a major mistake if time permits.
5. Aim for clean, representative attempts within the time limit.
6. Review your best lap in APEX.
7. Find the corner with the largest loss.
8. Focus on that corner in the next session.

extra.352: Run lower than default at Monza. Mid-range at Spa.
extra.353: Reduce lock from 75% to 65% to improve rotation mid-corner.
extra.354: Drop 1mm front to sharpen initial turn-in at fast corners.
extra.355: Move 0.5% rearward at Monza. Prevents early lock at T1.
extra.356: Target 27.5 PSI hot FL/FR. Rear 26.0 PSI.
extra.358: High rotation car that rewards aggressive driving style. More oversteer on power than Porsche. Faster raw pace but narrower operating window.
extra.359: Stiffen 1 click to control roll in fast corners.
extra.360: Increase preload 10Nm for better traction on exit.
extra.361: 1-2 clicks more than Porsche equivalent — needs download through fast corners.
extra.362: Reduce max pressure 5% — easily locks under heavy braking.
extra.363: Understeer-biased at turn-in but excellent traction car. Very forgiving, ideal for consistency training. Large tyre contact patch.
extra.364: Drop 2mm front to sharpen turn-in. Key for this car.
extra.365: Soften 1 click to add rotation on entry.
extra.366: Mid-range at all circuits. Stable but not draggy.
extra.368: Balanced GT3 with strong aero platform. Great at flowing circuits, less suited to tight technical tracks. Comfortable long-stint car.
extra.369: Higher than average. Car needs download to shine.
extra.370: 0.5% forward for better front bite at slow corners.
extra.372: Close the gap in Sector 2 at Monza. Focus on Lesmo entry and Ascari chicane exit.
extra.374: You're 60% through Braking Fundamentals. The exercise and practice task remain. Your data shows this is your biggest time loss.
extra.407: What single change gives me the most time right now?
extra.408: Explain my biggest braking problem in detail
extra.409: How do I improve my slow corner exit speeds?
extra.410: What does my low lines score mean?
extra.411: Should I fix braking or throttle application first?
extra.412: How much time am I losing per lap to my main issue?
extra.415: Apply brakes sharply at the start — full pressure in under 0.2s. This is the trapezoidal profile you should be seeing on the right.
extra.417: Fix a physical marker for your brake point in each corner. The variance between laps should be under 3 metres.
extra.419: Open the throttle at the speed minimum — not before and not more than 0.3s after. Earlier throttle means more speed down the following straight.
extra.421: The car needs to rotate before the apex, not after. A later apex allows a straighter exit line — which unlocks earlier throttle.
extra.423: Compare your speed trace lap to lap. The widening gap in the middle sector is your priority — one sector at a time.

landing.headline: Understand your driving through data.
landing.subhead: Compare laps, inspect braking and throttle inputs, and find what to practise next.
landing.engineering: From a recorded lap to a useful explanation.
landing.problem: A lap time tells you the result. APEX explores how telemetry can explain the driving decisions behind it.
landing.distanceBody: Laps are aligned by distance so differences in speed can be compared at corresponding points on the track.
landing.rulesBody: Telemetry rules identify input patterns and connect findings to Academy topics. The analysis depends on the channels available in the file.
landing.evidenceBody: The repository includes the analysis code, sample telemetry and automated checks for both interface languages.
landing.lessonBody: Explore how the point you aim for in a corner affects your exit. Then compare your throttle application and exit speed.
landing.author: Sole developer of APEX, built with the assistance of AI tools.
landing.research: To explore demand for the app, I reached out to active sim racing teams. The next research question is how useful the tool could be in their training process.
